analysis.one_liner: Withholds members of Congress's pay after October 1 unless Congress passes a budget and all spending bills.
analysis.headline: The No Budget, No Pay Act was introduced October 10, 2025 and referred to the House Committee on House Administration, where no action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill says that if Congress has not approved a budget resolution and passed all the regular spending bills by October 1 — the start of the federal fiscal year — members of Congress stop getting paid for however long the deadline is missed, with no back pay afterward. A small committee of the House and Senate budget and appropriations chairs would certify when members lose pay and when the noncompliance period ends. It would not take effect until September 2027, the final months of this Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill applies to every member of the House and Senate, who would forfeit pay for each day past October 1 without a completed budget and spending bills. In principle, the public benefits if the threat of lost pay pushes Congress to finish its spending work on time and avoid shutdowns, which can interrupt pay for federal workers and services people rely on. No outside group stands to gain money from the bill itself.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters expecting Congress to finish its budget work

how_it_helps.text: After October 1 of any fiscal year, no funds may be made available to pay any member of Congress for the period during which Congress has not approved a budget resolution and passed all regular appropriations bills, and no retroactive pay is allowed for that period [S3].
The House and Senate budget and appropriations chairs would certify, on October 1 of each fiscal year, whether Congress is in compliance and how many days members would go unpaid [S3].
Under current law, members continue receiving their pay during funding lapses, so the bill removes that protection and makes missing the deadline personally costly for members [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress bear the cost if the bill passes: they would forfeit pay for each day past October 1 that Congress has not completed a budget resolution and all regular appropriations bills, with no retroactive pay. Members are salaried officeholders — a category that includes many wealthy individuals — so the forfeited pay is likely a modest hardship for most and trivial for the wealthiest members. Taxpayers pay nothing extra; the bill does not create spending. If the pay threat actually induces Congress to finish budgets on time, federal workers and service recipients benefit from fewer shutdowns.

drawbacks.text: Members of Congress are not generally low-income; a salary withholding is a minor burden for wealthy members and a modest one for others, so the enforcement tool may be too weak to change behavior [S3].

The determination of whether Congress is in compliance is made by the budget and appropriations chairs themselves — the very committee leaders responsible for producing the budget and spending bills — giving those chairs significant control over when members lose pay [S3].

Members' pay is protected in the Constitution's Article I pay provision, and most 'no budget, no pay' schemes have been structured with delayed rather than forfeited pay for that reason; this bill instead prohibits payment outright and bars retroactive pay, which could invite a constitutional challenge, though the bill text does not address that question [S3].
No outside industry or interest group stands to gain money from this bill; the financial effect is limited to members' salaries [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's cost falls almost entirely on members of Congress, so in a narrow sense it is a low-cost accountability measure. Its real-world effect depends on whether withheld pay actually changes member behavior, which is doubtful given that many members are wealthy and salary withholding is a modest burden; constitutional questions around outright forfeiture of pay, rather than delayed pay, also make the mechanism legally uncertain. The strongest honest case for it is symbolic: it ties members' own pay to the budget work they routinely fail to finish on time.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Committee on House Administration, which has not acted on it, and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Moore (R-NC) introduced H.R. 5738 on October 10, 2025 with nine original cosponsors (eight Republicans and one Democrat) [S1, S4, S5].
The House referred the bill to the Committee on House Administration the same day; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill would take effect on September 29, 2027, near the end of the 119th Congress [S2, S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything: the bill has not moved past its referral to committee, and members of Congress continue to receive pay regardless of whether budgets pass on time.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 10, 2025 and has taken no further action on the bill in the record to date.

sides.party_line_note: Nine of the ten House sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans; one Democrat has joined, so support is mostly but not entirely one-sided.

industries.note: The bill would make members forfeit pay for every day past October 1 without a completed budget and spending bills, with no back pay. Members' own control over the legislative calendar means the outcome rests with the same officeholders it would penalize.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the House Committee on House Administration with no recorded action and modest bipartisan sponsorship (10 of 435 House members). Most bills referred to committee in this position never receive a markup or floor vote, and the effective date in late 2027 gives the committee no urgency; the likely path is that it expires at the end of the Congress without a vote.
